articles.title: Before Automating Everything, Ask This: Is Your Business Process Actually Ready for AI?
articles.excerpt: Before Automating Everything, Ask This: Is Your Business Process Actually Ready for AI? Artificial intelligence is changing how businesses approach everyday operations. From responding to customer inq…
articles.body: Before Automating Everything, Ask This: Is Your Business Process Actually Ready for AI? Artificial intelligence is changing how businesses approach everyday operations. From responding to customer inquiries to managing internal tasks, processing documents, and updating business systems, AI-powered automation is becoming increasingly accessible. Many companies are now exploring AI agents and workflow automation tools to reduce manual work and improve productivity. But there is an important question that businesses should ask before implementing any automation: Is the process actually ready to be automated? Because automating an unclear or poorly structured process does not necessarily make it better. Sometimes, it simply makes existing problems happen faster.
articles.author: Syed Ali

articles.title: Stop Deploying to ECS Just to See If Your Code Works
articles.excerpt: Originally published on metalbear.com. On ECS, the usual way to find out whether a change works is to deploy it. You build the image, push it, register a new task definition revision, wait for the rol…
articles.body: Originally published on metalbear.com . On ECS, the usual way to find out whether a change works is to deploy it. You build the image, push it, register a new task definition revision, wait for the rollout and look at what happened, then do it all again if it's wrong. A loop like that might have been tenable for humans, but a coding agent writes a change in seconds, then waits for a full rollout to learn whether it worked, and it rarely gets there on the first try. Most of the speed you got from the agent ends up spent on waiting for rollouts. Today we're launching mirrord for ECS. Your code can now run on your laptop, in your CI runner or in your coding agent's sandbox as if it were a live task in your staging environment, with the task's network, environment variables and IAM task role.
articles.author: Eyal Bukchin

articles.title: Why has it become harder and harder to type one-handed on smartphones these days?
articles.excerpt: Phones keep getting bigger, but our hands stay the same size. Phone3box. Its interface is almost starkly plain — just a large table listing over three thousand phone models, with height, width, thickn…
articles.body: Phones keep getting bigger, but our hands stay the same size. I’m not sure when it started, but every product launch now seems to compete over who has the larger screen, and reviewers keep talking about “immersive experience.” Yet a phone is, after all, something you hold in your hand. Spec sheets grow longer and longer, while hardly anyone talks about how comfortable it is to grip. It dawned on me later that the problem lies in the way we measure screens: inches refer to diagonal length, which barely tells you anything about how a phone feels in hand. What truly decides whether you can type one-handed is the body width. Two phones can both have a 6.7-inch display, yet one may be 75 millimetres wide and the other 78.
articles.author: cheng qian

articles.title: Semantic Cache with Redis to Cut AI API Costs
articles.excerpt: A semantic cache in Redis is the cheapest way to cut AI API costs in production, and it is also the easiest way to serve a confidently wrong answer to a customer who asked something slightly different…
articles.body: A semantic cache in Redis is the cheapest way to cut AI API costs in production, and it is also the easiest way to serve a confidently wrong answer to a customer who asked something slightly different. I have built both versions: the one that saved a company five figures a year, and the one that answered "how do I downgrade" with the enterprise upgrade instructions for three weeks before anyone noticed. The difference was not the vector index or the embedding model. It was whether the cache had a measured threshold, a versioned key, and a stated error budget.

articles.title: I Let AI Agents Rebrand My Entire OSS Ecosystem in One Night. Two Pipelines Were Silently Dead.
articles.excerpt: Two of my five repositories had delivery pipelines that were silently dead. Not failing loudly — dead. One site had served a two-week-old build while every deploy "ran". One repo had merged four PRs w…
articles.body: Two of my five repositories had delivery pipelines that were silently dead. Not failing loudly — dead . One site had served a two-week-old build while every deploy "ran". One repo had merged four PRs with zero CI checks since May. I found out because of a rebrand. In one night, AI agents and I merged 13 pull requests across those five repos and repainted it from Tailwind violet to burnt orange. Nothing surfaces a dead pipeline like finally shipping something you care about seeing. Merged is a feeling. Live is a measurement. Pipeline one. The ESLint docs site had a deploy workflow that had failed on every run for two weeks . The rebrand merged — 1,580 tests green — and production kept serving the violet build from mid-July.

articles.title: npm ERESOLVE: --legacy-peer-deps vs --force (What Each Really Does)
articles.excerpt: npm has two messages with "ERESOLVE" in them, and they're easy to mix up. One is an error and the install stops. The other is a warning and the install carries on. The usual advice for both is "add --…
articles.body: npm has two messages with "ERESOLVE" in them, and they're easy to mix up. One is an error and the install stops. The other is a warning and the install carries on. The usual advice for both is "add --legacy-peer-deps " or "add --force ", but the two flags don't do the same thing, and neither one fixes the conflict. I wanted to see exactly what each option does, so on 20 November 2026 I built a tiny conflict out of three local packages and installed it with npm 10.9.2, offline, so nothing came from the registry. A plugin wants kmg-lib@^1.0.0 as a peer dependency, and the project uses kmg-lib@2.0.0 . That's the same shape as a React 18 plugin in a React 19 app. Every output below is copied from that test. Where I couldn't observe something, I say so.

articles.body: Sauron is one of the most famous villains of all time, but The Lord of the Rings doesn’t really explore why the Dark Lord is so obsessed with conquering all of Middle-earth. The prequel series The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has been working to make Sauron (Charlie Vickers) more complex — which isn’t hard since he gets to have conversations with other characters rather than solely appear as an ominous eye. articles.excerpt: Auto Blocker is getting stricter with One UI 9.5 and scammers won't like it.
articles.body: Credit: Ryan Haines / Android Authority TL;DR With One UI 9.5, users won’t be able to change Auto Blocker settings during a call. This is to thwart scammers trying to get people to disable security features. The feature is already live in the first One UI 9.5 beta on the Galaxy S26. Samsung’s One UI comes with Auto Blocker , which warns you before sideloading APKs and protects your Galaxy phone or tablet from malicious execution over USB or from harmful files received via messaging apps. With One UI 9.5 beta that rolled out to the Galaxy S26 series earlier this week, Auto Blocker appears to be getting additional anti-scam features that prevent hackers from misguiding users during calls.

articles.title: 53 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Sci-Fi History Is Still The Best Book Quote Of The 1970s
articles.excerpt: Roadside Picnic ends with one of science fiction’s most beautiful lines, a simple wish for happiness that still resonates more than 50 years later.
articles.body: The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984 ’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Big Brother") to The Three-Body Problem ’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out. The best sci-fi endings don't offer comfortable closure. Instead, they reframe everything that came before. In their closing lines, great sci-fi novelists leave readers suspended in the aftermath, forced to stew in the terrifying logic of cold technology, the fragility of human nature, and the vast expanse of space.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.
